I am sort of stuck at this stage. Moving past the embarrassment of my mania holds me back from getting back out of my shell. I get so much accomplished when I am manic until I fall into the delusions and hallucinations. I feel guilty that I put my family and friends through this again. I do not want to be so shy anymore.

This is something that I still struggle with even though I've been on medication for years. I still have mild mood swings, and I get a lot done while manic, then nothing done while depressed. I'm also more of an asshole in both those moods in different ways. So, I tend to say things I don't necessarily mean, etc. I also am completely inconsistent, and have a hard time with long term things, including supporting myself.

When I was not on medication, though, it got to the point where the things I got done while manic were irrelevant. I would end up working on ridiculous projects for the bulk of the episode; I would alienate people; and when depressed I would alienate myself.

Do you take medication? Do you have a counselor? Are your family and friends supportive and understanding of your disorder?

Ultimately, I think that it's not worth worrying about friends and family unless your relationship with them is becoming unstable. Part of having relationships with other people is the bad times and most people can deal with that, and forgive. You could also talk to them about how you feel guilty. I don't know the type of relationships you have with them, but if you are comfortable with exposing that part of you, it might help to alleviate your guilt, and it might allow them to see that there are times where they should take caution with their judgement. In the end, though, you should realize that, despite how much they try, people will never truly be able to understand what it's like for you unless they, too, have bipolar disorder.

I have began the apologies and the responses have been positive to me. My mother sometimes blames herself, and I tell her not to. They (family and friends) are no more interested in playing that blame game any more than I am, so that has helped ease that guilt. I told my therapist about my guilt and embarrassment today and he smiled and basically told me that my family loves me no matter what. My SO and I going to see the therapist at a later date, so the he can be better educated with my disorder.

On the whole, I am looking at this latest manic episode (that included some major, dark delusions), as a learning experience and a huge wake-up call. I take my meds as prescribed and I see the therapist often. I did not take this mental illness as seriously before simply because I did not believe that the delusions could come back. I never thought that I could be so delusional.

The only person who has been a total dick to me was someone in HR at work who spoke to me disrespectfully about returning to work. However, I stood my ground and did not let that person talk down to me (small victories). Ultimately, it is down to me to do the explaining and be my own sort of patient advocate in these situations. And you are right, people who do not experience this disorder will not fully understand, but more often than not, I can try to help people understand or decide to walk away from those who refuse to even try to understand.

I hope the best for you. Getting stable and transitioning back into "normal" habits is difficult.

Offhand, I don't recall having any bad experiences when being honest about my disorder. I think sometimes my mom feels a little guilty for not noticing sooner that there was something wrong but, for various reasons, there were always more intuitive explanations - lazy, "just teenager things," etc. In the end I'm actually the one that went and got diagnosed while I was at college (for the second time.) I started not being able to keep up with grades in the classes I cared about and then was like "hmm, maybe something's wrong."

In some ways I'm actually jealous of your delusions, but maybe only in morbid curiosity. My highs and lows were getting pretty intense the several months preceding my diagnosis, but I never had any straight up fictitious delusions, just some twisted interpretation of the world and people's motives, etc.

I've been taking the same medication for 4 years, but the dosage has been increased twice. I actually need to go in sometime soon because I'm finding that it's starting to not work that well again. It's really quite frustrating, and people don't realize that just because I take medication doesn't mean that everything is magically better. I'm quite afraid to go off medication - if it's more intense now despite the meds, then I can't imagine what it would be like without them.

The annoying thing is that one of the things that really screws over my stability is stress, and the whole "having a job" thing stresses me out. I usually make it about four to six months before I start getting miserable and depressed. The only reason I was able to keep my last two jobs for more than a couple months is because they were places that were fairly lenient about missing days.

So, atm I am being like 60% supported by my family, which goes back to the whole guilt thing. But here I am, getting the support from them. I'm trying to do things for myself, but even setting up doctor appointments is really hard because I have such damn bad anxiety. I've always found it incredibly ironic that the anxiety prevents me from getting help with the anxiety.

I still remain hopeful, but as the years pass I feel like I might never be stable; that perhaps acceptable is the closest to normal I will get.

Some of my delusions and hallucinations were beautiful and I am actually sorta grateful for them. They prevented from doing worse things such as hopping on a plane and going on a physical trip or cheating on my SO or spending tens of thousands of dollars of things (although, I did purchase this laptop while manic, 0% interest, though). I think that I experienced synesthesia while manic and delusional. I would spend my waking hours listening to music. I closed my eyes and saw color before my eyes. I looked up at the ceiling and thought of stars and it would glow with a blanket of stars. I got in the mood to see fireflies, so I listened to Owl City's "Fireflies" and my room glowed with them. I knew that these things were not real at the time. I knew that it was all in my head, but I enjoyed it all the same. While listening to my playlists, I was convinced that the artists were playing just for me, live. Since getting out of the hospital, I can occasionally see colors when listening to music, but it comes in waves and doesn't happen all of the time.

The dark part of the delusions is that I became convinced that family friend hurt me as a child. It scares me to think that I could actually be so far gone that I could believe that I was molested as a child and my brain just covered up the details. No one IRL knows about that delusion except for a select few family members and my SO, and thank goodness because it was not true. I do not know why precisely my brain went there, but I think it has to do with my religious upbringing (that's complicated) and a callback to my first manic episode where I believed that my SO was replaced by some kind of identical imposter that raped me in the shower. The brain can be so powerful and yet so fragile at the same time.

I am also concerned about the right meds. In a week or so, I am going to see my psychiatrist about coming off of the anti-psychotic and onto a mood stabilizer. It sucks that the process is more or less trial and error. I wish that we could just take blood tests that would just tell us exactly what we need and just stay on them. I am taking the medication thing much more seriously now, so that I do not wind up back into the hospital. I have accepted that I will not meet someone else's "normal" but I can get back to feeling myself (maybe be better?). I just have to keep trying and take responsibility for what I have done and then move on. Easier said than done.

I've always found bipolar disorder to be a mix of good and bad. Given the choice I'm not even sure I would "get rid" of it. Sometimes even in depressed episodes I just think of things in a new way, or I write some good music or something. Often I have to go back and look at my insecurities while I was depressed because often they weren't true, but still - it gave me a different context for things. Mania was almost by definition good. I look back on some of the songs I've written and kinda wonder if I even can possibly make things that good anymore. In some ways I also appreciate having such diverse emotional states. It really helps me be able to be more empathetic with people, and I've helped more than one person through a difficult time in their life. On medication I certainly feel more like myself. I don't think I necessarily didn't before, but there was a large aspect of my life that was out of my control - this particularly effected me in regards to my interpersonal relationships.

I feel the same way. I haven't always had such clarity about my diagnosis and there have been points where I wanted nothing more than to just be "normal". But now I am seeing that I can accept the good with the bad. Now I just want to figure out how to tap into the creative side without being manic.
